conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during this stay. You were just admitted for nausea and vomiting again, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I just can’t keep anything down. I feel so sick every time I try to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood pressure was very high when you came in—194 over 94. That’s concerning. Did you notice any headaches or chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no chest pain or headaches. Just the nausea and throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. We’re giving you IV fluids to help with dehydration. Your lab work showed a high lactate level earlier—4.6—which suggests your body was under stress from not having enough fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lactate? Is that like acidosis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s called lactic acidosis. But after three liters of IV fluids, your lactate dropped to 1.0, which is normal. So that’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s good. But why does this keep happening? I was just here two days ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what we’re trying to understand. You have gastroparesis, which means your stomach empties slowly. But we’ve also noticed that sometimes vomiting happens right after you drink or eat, even if it’s small amounts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t help it. I just feel so full and sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But one of the nurses saw you induce vomiting after drinking water. Is that something you do when you feel anxious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I don’t know. Maybe. It just feels like the only way to stop the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I want you to know we’re not judging you. But induced vomiting can make everything worse—dehydration, acidosis, even high blood pressure. It’s a cycle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you think it’s in my head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. Your gastroparesis is real. But the way you respond—vomiting right after intake—suggests a behavioral pattern, possibly linked to anxiety. That’s why psychiatry has been consulted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed some appointments. I know I should go, but I get too anxious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. The important thing is recognizing it now. We can help you set up a new appointment before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but I didn’t vomit last night. I tried sipping water slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your blood pressure is better too—142 over 88 this morning. We’ve switched you from IV labetalol to oral meds: lisinopril and amlodipine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was on lisinopril before. Why the new one?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because your blood pressure was so high, we needed an extra medication. Amlodipine helps relax your blood vessels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my insulin? My sugars have been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you glargine at night and lispro with meals. Since you’re not eating much, we’re using a sliding scale to adjust doses safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had the gastric pacer for a reason. Why isn’t it helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pacer helps some, but it can’t override the effects of frequent vomiting or anxiety. We also discussed a J-tube, but you decided against it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want surgery. I just want to stop feeling like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And that’s possible. But it will take work—both medically and with mental health support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray yesterday was clear—no pneumonia or aspiration. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about that. I’ve thrown up so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. But your lungs look good. The main issue remains the cycle of vomiting, dehydration, and high blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking. Maybe the vomiting does help me feel temporary relief, but then I feel worse after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a really important insight. It’s like a coping mechanism, but it’s harming your body in the long run.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what can I do instead?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll work with psychiatry to find strategies—maybe different medications or therapy techniques to manage the urge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve gone two full days without vomiting. That’s a big improvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I still feel nauseous, but I’ve been using the Zofran and trying deep breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. And your labs are stable—no acidosis, hemoglobin is holding, and your electrolytes are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge tomorrow, yes. But we want to make sure you’re safe with follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll go to psychiatry this time. I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule it before you leave. And we’re giving you Zofran for breakthrough nausea, plus your regular Reglan and Nexium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take lisinopril 10 mg three times a day and amlodipine twice daily. We lowered the lisinopril dose to avoid low BP now that you’re hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. You’ve been off IV fluids for 24 hours, eating small meals, and no vomiting. How do you feel?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tired, but better. I’m scared it’ll come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. But you’ve made real progress by acknowledging the role of anxiety. That’s the first step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep working on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll support you. Discharge is set for tomorrow morning. Rest up, and the nurse will review your meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Remember: take your meds, eat small meals, and call if nausea returns. Most importantly—keep your psychiatry appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really want to get better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we believe you can. Take care.
